title: Relationship among ℕ, W, ℤ and ℚ
competency: Describe the relationship among the sets ℕ, W, ℤ and ℚ.

keywords.def: An item in a set. We write ∈ for "is an element of".
A drawing of circles that shows how sets are related.

en.text: Natural numbers sit inside the whole numbers. Whole numbers sit inside the integers. Integers sit inside the rational numbers. So a natural number like 10 is also whole, an integer and rational. A fraction like 1/7 is only rational.

am.text: የተፈጥሮ ቁጥሮች በሙሉ ቁጥሮች ውስጥ ናቸው። ሙሉ ቁጥሮች በኢንቲጀሮች ውስጥ ናቸው። ኢንቲጀሮች በሬሽናል ቁጥሮች ውስጥ ናቸው። ስለዚህ 10 ሙሉ፣ ኢንቲጀርና ሬሽናል ነው። 1/7 ግን ሬሽናል ብቻ ነው።

screens.title: Guess the smallest set
screens.text: Put each number in the smallest set it belongs to. Check against the figure after.
items: A fraction that is not an integer.

screens.title: Recall
paras: A collection of items is called a set.
The items in a set are called elements. We use the sign ∈.
A Venn diagram uses circles to show how sets are related.

screens.title: Each set sits inside the next
screens.ask: Tap a circle, then tap each number.
rings: Any a/b with a, b integers and b ≠ 0.
numbers: A natural number is in every set.
A fraction that is not an integer.

screens.title: Classifying a number
paras: When a set is inside a larger set, its numbers belong to the larger set too.
To classify a number, find its smallest set. It also belongs to every set around it.

screens.title: Classify −13 step by step
steps: Is −13 a counting number (1, 2, 3, …)? No, it is negative. So −13 ∉ ℕ.
Is it a whole number (0, 1, 2, …)? No, whole numbers are never negative. So −13 ∉ W.
Does it have a fraction part? No. So −13 is an integer: −13 ∈ ℤ.
ℤ sits inside ℚ, so −13 ∈ ℚ too.
Answer: −13 belongs to ℤ and ℚ.

screens.title: Key words
defs: An item in a set, shown with ∈.
A drawing of circles that shows how sets are related.

screens.text: Number sets: can a number be rational and whole, but not an integer?
screens.why:
Look at Figure 1.11: the W circle is inside the ℤ circle.
So every whole number is also an integer.
A whole number that is not an integer cannot exist.
Answer: No.
screens.clue: Look at Figure 1.11. Where is the W circle?

screens.title: Classify each number: which sets does it belong to?
items: A natural number is in every set.
screens.why:
Find the smallest set first, then add every set around it.
−13 is a negative integer: ℤ and ℚ.
1/7 and −5/76 are fractions that are not integers: only ℚ.
10 is natural, so it is in ℕ, W, ℤ and ℚ.
screens.clue: Is the number a fraction? Is it negative?

screens.text: Classify 0: Solomon says 0 belongs only to the rational numbers. What is his error?
opts: 0 is also whole and an integer
screens.ans: 0 is also whole and an integer
screens.why:
0 is not a counting number, so 0 ∉ ℕ.
But 0 is a whole number: 0 ∈ W.
W is inside ℤ and ℚ, so 0 ∈ ℤ and 0 ∈ ℚ too.
His error: 0 is also whole and an integer.

screens.text: Number sets: true or false? Every natural number is a whole number.
screens.why:
Natural numbers: 1, 2, 3, …
Whole numbers: 0, 1, 2, 3, …
Every natural number appears in the whole numbers.
So ℕ ⊂ W: true.

screens.text: Classify a mixed number: true or false? −3 2/7 belongs to the negative integers.
screens.why:
Integers have no fraction part: …, −4, −3, −2, …
−3 2/7 lies between −4 and −3.
It has the fraction part 2/7, so it is not an integer.
It is a negative rational number: false.

screens.text: Number sets: simplify first. Which numbers are in ℤ but NOT in W?
screens.why:
Simplify: 12/4 = 3 and −15/3 = −5.
0 and 3 are whole numbers, so they are in W.
−1/2 is not an integer at all.
−6 and −5 are negative integers: in ℤ but not in W.
Answer: −6 and −15/3.
screens.clue: Simplify each one. Negative integers are in ℤ but not in W.

items.text: Classify 0: Solomon says 0 belongs only to ℚ. Which is correct?
opts: 0 belongs to W, ℤ and ℚ
items.ans: 0 belongs to W, ℤ and ℚ
items.why:
0 is a whole number: 0 ∈ W.
W sits inside ℤ, and ℤ sits inside ℚ.
So 0 ∈ W, 0 ∈ ℤ and 0 ∈ ℚ.
0 is not natural, because counting starts at 1.

items.text: Number sets: true or false? The whole numbers and their opposites are called integers.
items.why:
Whole numbers: 0, 1, 2, 3, …
Their opposites: 0, −1, −2, −3, …
Together: …, −2, −1, 0, 1, 2, …
That is the set of integers ℤ: true.

items.text: Number sets: true or false? Every natural number is a whole number.
items.why:
ℕ = {1, 2, 3, …}.
W = {0, 1, 2, 3, …}.
Every element of ℕ is in W, so ℕ ⊂ W.
True.

items.text: Classify a mixed number: true or false? −3 2/7 belongs to the negative integers.
items.why:
−3 2/7 is between −4 and −3.
It has a fraction part, 2/7.
Integers have no fraction part.
So it is a rational number, not an integer: false.

test.text: Classify a number: what is the smallest set that contains −7?
test.why:
−7 is negative, so it is not in ℕ or W.
−7 has no fraction part, so it is an integer.
The smallest set is ℤ.
(It is also in ℚ, but ℚ is bigger than ℤ.)

test.text: Classify a number: what is the smallest set that contains 2/3?
test.why:
2/3 lies between 0 and 1.
There is no integer between 0 and 1, so 2/3 ∉ ℤ.
2/3 is a/b with b ≠ 0, so 2/3 ∈ ℚ.
The smallest set is ℚ.

test.text: Number sets: true or false? Every integer is a rational number.
test.why:
Any integer n can be written n/1.
For example −4 = −4/1 and 0 = 0/1.
The bottom is 1, which is not 0.
So every integer is rational: true.

test.text: Number sets: true or false? Every whole number is a natural number.
test.why:
0 is a whole number.
Natural numbers start at 1, so 0 is not natural.
One example is enough to break the rule.
So the statement is false.

test.text: Integers: simplify first. Which of these are integers?
test.why:
10/2 = 5, an integer.
−4 and 0 are integers.
3/2 = 1 1/2 and 2.5 have a fraction part.
Answer: −4, 0 and 10/2.
